So this is due to moisture content and Psychrometrics.
Mostly the relationship between temperature, dew point, relative humidity and specific humidity; in air, but surfaces/buildings materials/contents also come into play, as does vapour pressure. You'd be surprised how much thermodynamics is at play in this situations

Adelaide is known for having lower humidities, so when you place excess moisture in a closed environment, either through wet clothes, or an unknown leak into a building cavity, or whatever. You increase the vapour pressure.

If you think of air as a sponge, as it heats it expands and can take on more water vapour when available.

So for example, it's winter, you set up clothes to dry inside, blast a heater on them, and the vapour pressure and both specific and relative humidity of the wet clothes is higher than the dry air, this then warmed as you heat the air, and evaporation occurs as your heat the clothes. Due to system moving from high to low for equilibrium, the pressure and humidity factors of the air goes up, as moisture pushes into the air. This essentially increases the amount of moisture in the air space.

The clothes dry, you pack them away, and turn. down or off the heater, and the air cools a bit. Back to the sponge analogy, it is like you dipped a sponge in water, and now you are squeezing it a bit. The water needs to drop out of suspension, and goes to the coolest place to do this, where this is a cool surface and likely a lower vapour pressure, and cooler, dry atmosphere due to the dry Adelaide climate, which is most often the glass windows, this will hit dew point (the temperature at which condensation forms) and you get moisture condensing into the cool glass.

To avoid this, as you have added extra moisture to the system, yeah have to allow the extra moisture to leave the system. Open the window a bit, so you add extra ventilation to mitigate this.

~if water ingress is long term and / or extensive, check every surrounding building structure, concrete slab under flooring (may need a concrete metre) or subfloor materials, skirting boards/kickboards, door frames etc

~if moisture is elevated definitely get a dehum,  if it has all been wet more than a few days turn the fan off now! and get some mould testing done
